answers: Earlier this year, President Trump noted "I just don't want a poor person" in charge of economic posts in his administration, then touted Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross as "a very rich person" who was up to the task. But just how rich Ross really is is now up in the air, Forbes reports, noting it's yanked Ross off its billionaires list after a one-month probe revealed that $2 billion or so or Ross' alleged fortune "never existed," and that Ross had engaged in an "apparent sequence of fibs, exaggerations, omissions, fabrications, and whoppers" with the magazine going back 13 years. The discovery came when Ross, 79, contacted Forbes in October to refute his ranking: Last year he was listed with a net worth of $2.9 billion on the Forbes 400; he claimed he was worth closer to $3.7 billion. Then Forbes talked with 10 of Ross' ex-employees at his private equity firm, who noted a "penchant for misleading" that affected fellow workers and investors and spurred big fines, suits, and refunds to backers. "Wilbur doesn't have an issue with bending the truth," one longtime colleague says, while another is more blunt: "He's lied to a lot of people." The magazine delves into Ross' back story, including how, when he first made the Forbes billionaires list in 2004 with a net worth of $1 billion, "everyone that I knew that worked with Wilbur knew it wasn't true," per a former colleague. When Forbes told Ross he was being removed from its billionaires club, Ross retorted the magazine wasn't counting family trusts that he wasn't obligated to inform the feds about—in the amount of "more than $2 billion," assets Ross said he put into the trusts sometime "between the election and [my] nomination." When Forbes asked to see a paper trail proving that, Ross cited "privacy issues"—and the magazine lays out other problems with Ross' story on the supposed $2 billion transfer. In late 2017, Forbes magazine published a detailed investigation into the financial disclosures of Wilbur Ross, the U.S. Secretary of Commerce under President Donald Trump. The article revealed that Ross had long exaggerated his net worth, initially claiming to be worth $3.7 billion, while his official financial disclosures showed significantly less. Forbes found that Ross had transferred over $2 billion in assets to family trusts between the 2016 presidential election and his nomination to the Cabinet, a move he claimed allowed him to avoid disclosing those assets. However, Forbes concluded that the $2 billion never existed, and Ross had lied to maintain a higher public image.

The article traced Ross' career, highlighting his rise as a top bankruptcy negotiator in the 1990s, his success in the private equity world with WL Ross & Co., and his eventual sale of the firm to Invesco in 2006. Despite his firm's success, Ross was known for misleading investors, colleagues, and even Forbes, often inflating his net worth to attract more capital. His financial misrepresentations led to legal issues, including a $2.3 million fine from the SEC and the refund of $11.8 million to investors.

Ross' appointment as Commerce Secretary came with the requirement to disclose his assets, which he did in 2015, listing a total of $3.4 billion. However, Forbes later adjusted his net worth to $2.9 billion, and Ross continued to claim higher figures. His refusal to provide documentation and his insistence that the $2 billion transfer to trusts was legitimate raised ethical concerns, especially given his role in the Trump administration.

In a separate news piece, President Trump defended his decision to appoint Ross, stating that he wanted a wealthy individual to lead the Commerce Department, arguing that "rich people" are better suited for economic roles. Trump emphasized that Ross and other high-profile appointees had to give up significant wealth for their positions, and he claimed that his administration was composed of the "best and brightest," despite the controversy surrounding Ross' financial disclosures.

The two news passages together paint a picture of a political figure whose career has been marked by financial opacity, legal challenges, and a public image that often diverges from reality. Ross' appointment to the Cabinet, while controversial, reflects Trump's broader strategy of appointing wealthy individuals to key roles, a move that has drawn both support and criticism.

In late 2017, Forbes magazine investigated the financial disclosures of Wilbur Ross, the U.S. Secretary of Commerce under President Donald Trump. Ross had long claimed to be a billionaire, with Forbes listing his net worth at around $2.9 billion in 2016. However, after reviewing his financial disclosures, Forbes concluded that Ross had significantly overstated his wealth. Ross had previously claimed his net worth was as high as $3.7 billion, but the actual value of his assets, based on official filings, was much lower—less than $700 million. 

Ross contested Forbes' findings, arguing that he had transferred over $2 billion in assets to family trusts, which he claimed were not required to be disclosed in his federal filings. He insisted that these assets were not part of his personal wealth and that he had always been transparent with Forbes. However, Forbes found no evidence to support the claim of a $2 billion transfer, suggesting that Ross had fabricated the story to justify his high net worth listing. 

The controversy surrounding Ross' financial disclosures raised questions about his ethics and transparency, especially given his role in the Trump administration. The Department of Commerce denied the existence of the $2 billion transfer, and Ross' team claimed he had always complied with all legal and ethical standards. Despite this, the episode highlighted a pattern of financial misrepresentation that had persisted for years, with Ross' former colleagues and investors alleging that he had misled them with inflated figures.

The controversy also intersected with broader political themes. President Trump defended Ross' appointment, arguing that he wanted to appoint wealthy individuals to key economic roles, stating that "rich people" were better suited to lead the economy. Trump emphasized that Ross and other high-profile appointees had given up significant personal wealth for their government positions, and he framed his administration as one that prioritized economic growth over political correctness.

The story of Wilbur Ross' financial disclosures reflects a larger narrative about wealth, power, and transparency in American politics. It raises questions about the integrity of public figures, the role of media in holding them accountable, and the ethical implications of wealth in governance. As the Trump administration continued to face scrutiny, the Ross case became a symbol of the challenges in balancing personal wealth with public service.
